newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia says tax no bar to deep water oil search.
newsitem.headline: Australia says tax no bar to deep water oil search.

text.p: Australian Resources and Energy Minister Warwick Parer said on Monday he disagreed with claims by petroleum producers that the current tax regime for deep water drilling was an impediment to exploration growth.
"I don't agree with that," Parer told reporters after addressing the Australian Petroleum Production and Exploration Association Ltd (APPEA) conference.

Nick Heath, a director of Esso Australia Ltd and chairman of APPEA, said the government would be presented with a proposal later this year, outlining changes it would like to see in the taxing structure.
Unlike in other highly prospective areas, such as the Gulf of Mexico and the North Sea, where tax breaks are given for deep-water drilling, Australia's tax is uniform regardless of the depth.
Heath said the intent of the paper would be to outline steps needed to ensure Australia's exploration potential is fully exploited in future years.
"What we'll be saying to the government is 'let's see how we can maximise deep water drilling'," Heath said.
Mike Baugh, general manager of petroleum, Australasia, for The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd said the proposal would be presented to the government in May.
"We'll roll out the proposal as what we think needs to be different," Baugh said.
In releasing its latest industry survey this week, APPEA cited high levels of taxation as dampening the industry's overall performance.

However, Parer said he believed Australia's tax regime for deep water exploration was competitive with other countries and that Australia was increasingly regarded as highly prospective for both domestic and foreign investors.
APPEA has so far stopped short of directly lobbying the Federal government for deep water tax breaks.
However, APPEA executive director Barry Jones said declining industry profits were a worrying trend.
After-tax returns on assets declined in 1995/96 to 7.2 percent from 8.3 percent the previous year on an industry wide basis, APPEA figures show.
It was the fourth successive year of falling returns.
"A continuation of this current trend of lower returns must be a cause of concern to industry participants, investors and government," Jones said.
Petroleum industry taxes totalled A$2.645 billion in 1995/96, up three percent from the previous year, APPEA figures show.
